scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4630: HELP! The workstation it_lab3, one of the IT lab
machines on 192.168.1.x, has turned into a complete BRICK. It can't reach
anything at all, not even its own gateway thing. Something around its port on
the lab switch must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone move it to
a working port and make it talk to the network again!! The student who uses it
is just sitting there!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. it_lab3 has its IP on 192.168.1.0/24, reaches its
  gateway (192.168.1.1) with 0% loss, and RIP is converged so it reaches other
  segments too. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a single-host isolation that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- it_lab3 is totally isolated
and cannot reach even its gateway -- is NOT reproducible: it_lab3 holds its
192.168.1.0/24 address, reaches its default gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss, and
(RIP being converged on router0/router1/router2) reaches off-segment destinations as
well.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: it_lab3 is fully connected and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the it_lab3 -> gateway path
(and an off-segment ping), finds it working, checks the host's interface/route, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dead port or isolated host to satisfy the
ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The helpdesk report that it_lab3 is a "complete brick" unable to reach its gateway is not supported by live evidence. A direct ping from it_lab3 to its gateway (192.168.1.1 on router0.eth0) returned 2/2 responses with 0% loss and ~1.2 ms RTT, confirming the path is healthy.

The misleading observable that prompted the report was it_lab3's TX packet counter showing zero. This is the normal idle baseline for a freshly started Kathara container that has not yet been asked to send any traffic — no application, cron job, or interactive user had generated outbound packets since lab initialization. The counter incremented correctly the moment a ping was issued. The same TX=0 pattern was confirmed on other idle hosts (it_lab2, it_hod, cs_lab1), establishing it as a topology-wide startup baseline, not a per-host fault.

The full diagnostic sweep found nothing wrong: infra_sweep flagged 0 devices across all 30 (no ACL rules, no addressing errors, no gateway divergence); tc_snapshot showed pfifo_fast clean on every interface; l2_snapshot duplicates were the standard kernel tunnel-interface zero-MACs present on every Linux host; pressure_sweep reported 0 suspect devices; and router0's routing table correctly carries the IT LAN (192.168.1.0/24), CS LAN (192.168.2.0/24), and WAN (10.0.0.0/8) prefixes. There is no fault to repair.

Root cause: no fault exists — the TX=0 counter was an idle-startup baseline, not a network failure. The student's workstation is connected and functional; no port move is necessary.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes it_lab3 holds its address and reaches its gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent demonstrated a successful ping from it_lab3 to 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss, confirming baseline connectivity and implying the host retains its IP address.

The agent's probes (direct ping from it_lab3 to its gateway, host interface snapshots, infra/l2/pressure sweeps, and router routing table) in the log support the conclusion that the reported isolation is not reproducible. One minor unshown detail (an explicit post-ping TX counter read) is asserted but does not undermine the overall evidence set.
